item.title: Fake polls are a real problem
item.description: They’re nothing new, but they may be a growing threat. Plus, the story of the 2026 campaign through political ads in Still Counting EP7.
item.content:encoded:
Still Counting Episode 7 is ready. This episode is a little bit on the longer side. The original plan was to tell the story of the 2026 campaign through the ubiquitous ads that you’re undoubtedly seeing if you’re in a swing state. But then a bunch of polling-related news broke shortly before taping, such as a New York Times/Siena University poll showing strong numbers for Democrats on the generic ballot, and a scandal involving a fake “polling” firm called Wedgewood Polls.

I’ll have some extensive commentary about Wedgewood later in this post. But first, here’s the Still Counting video…

And here’s the audio. Once again, we’re very grateful for your reviews, comments, likes and subscribes.


The context

In 2009, I published a story at FiveThirtyEight suggesting that the prolific polling firm Strategic Vision was probably faking its data. It might have been a dumb risk. I never vetted the story with a lawyer, though I had asked Strategic Vision for comment, and their cagey responses reinforced my view that something weird was going on.

I thought the case was highly convincing, however. (I guess back then, I applied more of a “big forgiveness rather than ask permission” mindset.) Strategic Vision “polls” exhibited statistical patterns — namely, being far more likely to contain some trailing digits (such as 5, 7, 8 and 9) than others, including on obscure questions they probably thought would never be scrutinized — that were canonical signs of forged election results in authoritarian regimes. (Human beings are pretty bad at picking truly random numbers.) It was extremely unlikely these results had emerged by chance alone. My “spidey sense” also told me something was a little off about Strategic Vision’s results — though I forget exactly which details led me to that hypothesis.

But I was right — or at least I think that’s a reasonably safe assumption based on their subsequent behavior. The American Association for Public Opinion Research censured Strategic Vision for failing to disclose methodological information, and Strategic Vision never really attempted to provide any convincing refutation. They packed up their tent and left the industry.

The next year, in 2010, “polls” from another prolific firm, Research 2000, were discovered to contain similar anomalies. Research 2000 fought back a little harder, sending me a cease-and-desist letter, but Daily Kos, whom they were “polling” for at the time, sued them before they, too, disappeared. This was actually a bigger scandal than Strategic Vision. Research 2000 had frequently conducted “polls” for local newspapers and news outlets, presumably for a healthy amount of compensation.

Subscribe now

Earlier this week, Wedgewood Polls admitted it had fabricated data. It claimed its “polls” were an “experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern political polling industry.”

My opinion is that Wedgewood’s explanation is bullshit, a pathetic attempt to get ahead of the story after FiftyPlusOne was set to publish a story exposing the fraud. Whether some sort of crime was committed was unclear — Wedgewood allegedly collected crowdfunded money for a poll that may or may not have ever been conducted.1 FiftyPlusOne reports that Wedgewood identified Jack Sims and Andrew Prater as the people behind the firm. Whoever was responsible for fabricating the data probably shouldn't be trusted with anything election- or poll-related again.

These “polls” had made their way into FLIPR, although they weren’t having much influence on the model. When we removed them from our database yesterday, FLIPR’s various averages and forecasts were basically unchanged. That’s a bit confounded because a lot of polls are coming out these days, including a strong series of generic ballot polls for Democrats published before yesterday’s update. Still, FLIPR includes precautions against being overly influenced by any one poll, and new/unknown pollsters start with fairly low ratings by default.

For what it’s worth, here were the Wedgewood “polls” that had entered our database, as compared to the Silver Bulletin averages at the time.

There’s a slight D-leaning “house effect” here, though it’s pretty mild and not particularly consistent. In races where Silver Bulletin was publishing polling averages (there are a couple of caveats here: see the footnote2), their “polls” were about 0.6 points more favorable to the Democratic candidate on average.

Wedgewood showed progressive candidates “polling” especially strongly

One thing that’s a bit unusual is that Wedgewood “polled” several races where there was little or no publicly-available polling at the time. At Silver Bulletin, we turn on the average for a race once there are three distinct polls from at least two distinct polling firms. Four races where Wedgewood issued a “poll” did not meet that distinction. As far as I can tell, in fact, Wedgewood was the first firm of any kind to “poll” Troy Jackson’s race against Susan Collins in Maine as Graham Platner was preparing to drop out; they had Jackson ahead by 5 points.

In Michigan, meanwhile, Wedgewood was relatively early to “poll” Abdul El-Sayed’s race against Mike Rogers, showing him ahead by 5 points, better than the average3 which had AES ahead by 0.4 points instead. A Democratic candidate who dropped out, Mallory McMorrow, has alleged that Wedgewood’s “polls” hurt donor and voter confidence in her campaign.

In the table, I’ve only listed polls that included the eventual general election nominees because I’m not sure how comprehensive our data is on candidates who lost their primaries. Though an early July Wedgewood “poll” did have Francesca Hong leading by 3 points in the general election against Tom Tiffany in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race when other polls at the time showed the race roughly tied.

So there is something of a pattern here of Wedgewood showing better numbers for notably progressive candidates than the consensus, although it’s hard to know how much to make of three races. Not all of their “polls” ran in this direction, however. In Nebraska, they published a September “poll” showing incumbent Republican Gov. Jim Pillen ahead by 17 points against Democrat Lynne Walz, when subsequent polls have shown the race much closer.

Overall, compared with past fake pollsters — which often tried to fit in rather than draw attention to themselves — the Wedgewood “polls” were a bit more narrative-shaping. Though I also wouldn’t overstate this. Before news of the scandal broke on Tuesday, I was vaguely aware of an entity called “Wedgewood Polls” but couldn’t have told you anything about them beyond that. We tend not to dissect individual polls very much at Silver Bulletin4, especially when they come from polling firms we’ve never heard of. And we’d encourage others to take that approach, too. I generally object to focusing too much on any single polling result. Outlier polls tend to receive more attention than polls that align with the consensus. This isn’t necessarily bad because the alternative is too much herding. But there’s no longer any obviously correct, gold-standard way to conduct a poll. “Just plug it into the average” isn’t a perfect heuristic — there are certain polls I find dubious for various reasons. And our averages weight established pollsters with good track records more heavily. But it’s probably the least-worst alternative versus applying some sort of subjective filter to polls, which may reflect an aggregator’s rooting interests or other biases.

Polls are being vetted, actually

How did the Wedgewood data enter our model in the first place?

The literal answer is that we take our polling data from The New York Times, subject occasionally to some manual additions and overrides. This has several advantages. The NYT feed is fast, comprehensive, and staffed by highly skilled professionals. And contrary to what the Wedgewood fraudsters have alleged, the Times does a lot of vetting. (The NYT didn’t include polls from another fake polling firm, Median Strategies, for instance.) In addition, the NYT feed is fairly explicitly modeled on the old FiveThirtyEight database schema and their criteria for poll inclusion, which I helped to design. So it doesn’t make a lot of sense to recreate their efforts when they’re basically already doing the work in basically the same way that we’d do it.

But what are those “manual additions and overrides”? They fall into a couple of categories. We have a list of 11 permanently banned pollsters whom we know or believe the preponderance of evidence suggests fabricated data or engaged in other gross misconduct — our opinion, not necessarily “proof beyond a reasonable doubt”. Most of these polling firms, like Strategic Vision and Research 2000, are no longer active or are rejected by the NYT feed anyway, but FLIPR just ignores them if they enter our database.

On top of that, we have another set of polling firms we consider “nonprofessional.” We aren’t accusing these polls of being fake; we just think they don’t meet the standard of scientific polls. The official Silver Bulletin rule is as follows:

We don’t use DIY polls commissioned by nonprofessional hobbyists on online platforms such as Google Surveys.

As a result, we exclude certain pollsters, like from SoCal Strategies5 and ActiVote, that are sometimes accepted by other polling aggregators. I’m not sure that I’m eager to discuss these choices on a case-by-case basis. If we flag a polling firm as “nonprofessional,” they’ll almost inevitably lobby us and make their case. Sometimes we find this convincing, and sometimes we don’t. On the other hand, we manually add polls from Rasmussen Reports, which aren’t listed by the NYT, owing to a legacy decision by the post-Nate version of FiveThirtyEight that we strongly disagree with.

We will also sometimes add polls if we catch them right before publication of our daily update, and the NYT hasn’t added them yet. But generally, we’re not doing a lot of this. If the NYT hasn’t listed a poll, it may be because it didn’t pass their vetting.6 None of this is that urgent, and we’d rather wait a day or two to see whether the NYT and other aggregators have included the poll lest we add some fake or nonprofessional datapoint.

What Silver Bulletin generally hasn’t been doing, though, is conducting “secondary screening” once a poll passes through the equivalent of the TSA security perimeter — meaning the NYT database. And that’s because the NYT usually does a very good job with its vetting. As the New York Times explained in an editor’s note, when new pollsters enter their database, they’re subject to a fair amount of scrutiny including emails and phone calls.

Of course, someone willing to fake a poll may also be willing to fake answers in response to a vetting process. And this is probably getting easier because of AI (although AI can plausibly also help with fraud detection). Ultimately, thanks to the smart work of FiftyPlusOne, this particular scam was caught, however.

No vetting process is going to bat 1.000, however. What’s wrong with taking an incredibly strict policy? Well, if you were a frequent flier after September 11, you probably know. Vigorous screening can waste time for the vast majority of people doing nothing wrong. And overly strict screening can produce a lot of false positives and contribute to racial or other sorts of profiling.

At the same time, the American aviation system just doesn’t let people board planes without passing through some sort of screening process. It’s not quite “guilty until proven innocent,” but boarding a commercial airline is treated as a privilege and not a right.

Polling is roughly like that too. Overall, within the broader polling/forecasting community, there’s probably more screening and vetting than there was several years ago. New/unknown pollsters do not enter the NYT database without passing through a vetting process, and most of the other aggregators follow a similar if less formal approach7, including Silver Bulletin in cases where we maintain our own original database.8

Are fake polls becoming more common?

So the industry is doing vetting and screening. But should the magnetometers be tuned to a more sensitive setting?

Probably. FiftyPlusOne’s G. Elliott Morris says his team will uncover other potential frauds soon too.

Meanwhile, as I wrote above, I’m not a big fan of amateur/DIY polls and we strive not to include them, but that’s a different problem from fraud.

Because we’re so close to the midterm date, I don’t expect the various polling aggregators to revisit their policies now, but it’s safe to assume there will be a lot of discussions about this before 2028.

But while fake polls are nothing new — indeed, there are probably some other Strategic Vision/Research 2000-type cases in the historical database that have never been detected — there are a couple of new risks.

One of them is publishing fake polls to manipulate prediction markets. Prediction markets have also been around for a long time but have far higher trading volumes now, potentially making for more profitable trades.9 I don’t know what Wedgewood’s motivations were. But publishing out-of-consensus “polls” or fake polls in sparsely-surveyed races have more potential to move markets.

Another motive might be to discredit the polling industry overall. President Trump and the White House, after all, have frequently used the term “fake polls” to refer to entirely valid polls when they show poor numbers for Republicans.

And as I wrote above, I expect to see various AI-assisted schemes and scams in every industry, including polling.

Still, the proprietors of poll-collection and forecasting websites are less naive than Wedgewood alleges. People in the industry know the data really well, and from Strategic Vision to Wedgewood, everyone has caught their share of scams at some point. Our instincts about when something doesn’t pass muster are usually pretty good. Or at least, so we’d like to think. The smartest cheaters are the ones who never get caught.

Silver Bulletin news & notes

Look for more about this soon, but we’re planning on co-hosting our election night coverage with The Argument and GD Politics, plus a number of special guests including Still Counting’s Clare Malone. We’re not planning on building an Election Night model — it would be hard to do better than the NYT “Needle” anyway — but we should have a deeply knowledgeable set of panelists to cover both granular details and big-picture takeaways.

Full disclosure: we need to test-drive the tech setup to figure out exactly what will be possible and what won’t. So no promises on the format just yet. Parts of the coverage will be reserved for paying subscribers, in case that’s any extra incentive to subscribe during what’s sure to be an exciting final 12 days of the campaign.

Subscribe now

1

Wedgewood claims the crowdfunded Nebraska poll was real even though the rest of their numbers were fake.

2

In these cases, I’ve used our average from the day before the final date that the Wedgewood “poll” was in the field. That ensures that the average wasn’t affected by the Wedgewood data itself. For example, if Wedgewood conducted a “poll” from Oct. 8-9, I’ve listed the average as of Oct. 8 because sometimes new polls are added quickly and can enter our averages on the same day as the final field date. Note that we began publishing our averages and FLIPR on Aug. 11 this year. For dates before then, I’ve used our retrospectively-calculated polling averages instead, as these generally closely resemble the averages at other polling websites.

3

Or really our retrospectively-calculated average since, as noted above, our polling averages launched on Aug. 11. There were plenty of other aggregators that had Michigan polling averages up at the time, however, and it was polling roughly as a toss-up at that time.

4

I’ll admit that we sometimes make exceptions for NYT/Siena since they’re among our most highly-rated pollsters and reliably provide an independent point of view.

5

Sims previously worked at SoCal Strategies, which has, perhaps suspiciously, gone offline.

6

Speed was much more of an issue in 2024, when we relied on the feed from the resource-starved version of FiveThirtyEight instead as our first pass.

7

There is probably some degree of profiling here, to be fair. A poll published on a website from a high-prestige academic institution that hasn’t conducted political surveys before is going to get less vetting than a poll listed on X from a group of people nobody has ever heard of.

8

While we rely on the NYT feed for midterms “horse race” polls — meaning, polls for Senate, gubernatorial and House races — we maintain our own database of presidential approval polls, generic ballot polls, and certain other polling series.

9

I’m an advisor to Polymarket.

item.title: The cognitive dissonance election
item.description: Democrats like what the polls say. They’re just not sure they believe them. Plus, Still Counting EP8 and our Election Night plans.
item.content:encoded:
This is the weekly Still Counting post. It’s coming to you a day late because yesterday was one of those days. Not in a bad way, but in the way the last few days before the election typically are.

We’re in a mode now where we’re sort of a tapas restaurant and are going to deliver posts to you as they become available from the overburdened kitchen. We’ll try to space things out, but it’s possible that dishes will pile up and there will be some dry spells, or that you’ll get more than one newsletter or more than one FLIPR update in a day.

The one constraint that’s absolutely locked into place is our Election Day coverage:

  • In line with FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin tradition, shortly after midnight on Tuesday, we’ll run the final FLIPR update of the season and post our final overview of the race.1

  • Then we’ll lie in bed “sleeping” as we refresh Twitter constantly.

  • We’ll spend the afternoon nervously pacing around while trying to ignore anecdotal reports about turnout in Waukesha County.

  • Then starting at roughly 5:30 pm, we’ll be co-hosting an Election Night video stream and liveblog with The Argument, Galen Druke’s GD Politics and Matt Yglesias’s Slow Boring, plus plenty of special guests. Like it says on the invites to cool parties (not that I’d know anything about those) we’ll go from 5:30 until “late,” although we’ll preserve some energy if the outcome is ambiguous and it looks like vote-counting has slowed to a crawl.

We tested the liveblogging tech last night, and it went relatively smoothly. We’re super excited about this feature, and grateful to Substack for developing it. We hope to employ it for things other than Tuesday too, like big political or sports nights.

The intent for Election Night is for the video stream to be free, while the liveblog, where we’ll get a bit more granular, will be for paying subscribers.2 We really hope that you’ll join us!

Subscribe now

Meanwhile, here’s the YouTube of the Still Counting episode:

And here’s the audio. We’re very grateful for any reviews, comments, likes and subscribes you might spare.

The context

When FLIPR launched in August, I wrote that this wasn’t an election that filled me with a sense of “existential dread,” compared with… well, most of the recent ones. We knew both background conditions and midterm history were on Democrats’ side. If anything, those indicators have been unusually self-consistent this cycle. It was safe to assume Democrats were clear favorites to flip the House — you didn’t need FLIPR to tell you that, really, considering that Republicans started out with such a small majority — along with a number of governorships and state legislatures.

But in the Senate, we were caught between the proverbial rock and a hard place, since the battlegrounds required for a Democratic majority were being contested in very red terrain. Were Democrats really going to win Texas? Or Kansas? Or Alaska?

FLIPR initially forecasted the Senate odds at close to 50/50. As in 2024, that had seemed to make this election something of a low-stakes affair for the model. 28,000 lines of code, and all FLIPR was really saying is “well, who knows?”

Then, within a couple of weeks of Labor Day, there was some kind of phase change, with Democrats gaining 2 to 3 points on the generic ballot. There were several logical reasons for this: rising gas prices, further declines in Trump approval, growing evidence of a Democratic enthusiasm advantage, and perhaps increased public concern about AI, an issue where Trump is on the wrong side of the consensus.

So we’re no longer in the safe, nothing-ventured, nothing-gained “toss-up” zone. Democrats moved up to being roughly 3-to-1 favorites in FLIPR, and they’ve basically remained there for a few weeks now.

If you squint, there’s actually been the slightest recovery for Republicans on the generic ballot — but I’d argue that state and district polls have, if anything, been getting better for Democrats, like in a set of CNN polls yesterday morning that had them winning Kansas by 4 points and Texas by 6 (!). Even South Carolina might be in play, a flip I was (and to some degree remain) skeptical about.

Don’t believe polls from CNN or the NYT? Well, look at the New York Times polling database, where we get most of FLIPR’s data from, and search for any poll showing “Republican sponsor.” The GOP-commissioned polls3 imply a Senate map that is at best a toss-up for Republicans, but really leaning D, along with deep prospective gains for Democrats in the House and bad results for Republicans in swing-state governorships.

In a twist that I’m not sure I’ve seen before, Republican “vibes” about this election — especially if you adjust those partisan polls for the usual partisan bias4 — almost seem to imply a worse outcome for Republicans than Democratic ones.

But just look at where Republicans are spending money: it implies a deeply defensive, almost “prevent defense” posture. Or look at how Democrats are trying to expand the map in the House. There’s some kind of disconnect here between stated beliefs and revealed preferences.

I don’t have as much time to go into a deep-dive about the psychology here as I’d like. But I think Democrats are treating the possibility of flipping the Senate as "found money.” They’re optimistic-ish, but they don’t want to get their hopes up too much. It’s easy to understand why:

  • 2016

  • Despite Joe Biden’s win that year, 20205

  • And to a slightly lesser extent, 2024

Still, it’s one thing to take a healthy attitude of “hope for the best, but be prepared for the worst,” and another to actually have to put odds on the outcome, as FLIPR and people trading at prediction markets do. Some of the gaps between models and markets that we’ve previously highlighted have narrowed significantly.

But it remains hard to wrap your head around this election because it feels so boom-or-bust:

This is an understandable sentiment, and the “boom” part is true. Conditional upon James Talarico winning in Texas — Texas! — Democrats will be huge favorites to flip the Senate. Specifically, around 90 percent of the time according to FLIPR Deluxe.

But if Democrats don’t win Texas?

What might be counterintuitive is that they’ll retain decent chances of winning the Senate. Democrats could flip the Senate solely by winning states that Barack Obama won at least once: North Carolina, Maine, Ohio and Iowa. (They’d also, nontrivially, have to hold all of their own seats.) There are also more exotic possibilities: Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, South Carolina or maybe even Montana.

FLIPR polling averages show Mary Peltola and Adam Hamilton slightly ahead in Alaska and Kansas, respectively. Nebraska is basically a tie in the polls between Pete Ricketts and Dan Osborn, although the advanced features of FLIPR shift Nebraska to Lean R.

But here’s where I think some of the cognitive dissonance creeps in. It’s easy to say: “well, either there will be a polling bust” — indeed, such an occurrence is highly plausible! — or “polls are basically right, so Democrats will win and maybe run up the score.” Ergo, the Senate is 50/50, you might think.

That’s not the worst first approximation, but it leaves a lot out. Those outcomes aren’t necessarily equally likely, and this election isn’t necessarily that binary. Democrats might be able to withstand a modest polling error in the Senate. Or polls could underestimate them, like they did in 2025.

Or the outcome might just get a bit weird. I wouldn’t really be that surprised, for instance, if Talarico wins — but Susan Collins wins too.

Election observers might actually be overindexing to presidential years, when there are the same two candidates on the ballot at the top of the ticket, and race-by-race correlations are stronger than in midterms. Because they lead in the polls, however narrowly, in states totaling 54 Senate seats — 55 if you count Nebraska, where Osborn is 0.3 points “ahead” in our polling average6 — most of the weird outcomes result in D wins, in the same way that being a field goal ahead is nice if the second half of an NFL game turns into a comedy of errors.

At the same time, there isn’t any sort of “safe space” here. There’s no “Blue Wall” or anything like that. Except probably for North Carolina, none of the prospective D pickups are “safe” or “solid.” I have my opinions about which pickups are relatively more likely and relatively less likely, and FLIPR does too.

But this requires a willingness to “trust the process,” when Democrats very understandably feel like the polls are Lucy with the Football. And even FLIPR can only provide conditional, probabilistic affirmation. A roughly 3-in-4 chance means that you’ll lose 1 in 4 times: all it takes is the coin coming up tails twice in a row.

It’s more natural to compare 2026 to other midterms. But in certain ways, the best analogy is to a presidential year, 2008, the last time the political environment was polling so blue. Barack Obama flipped several states — Virginia, Colorado, North Carolina and oddly, Indiana — that at the time were considered canonically, almost existentially Republican. (Those states have taken different trajectories since then, obviously.) Or if you prefer, FLIPR’s forecast is a bit like picking the Knicks to win the NBA title or the Milwaukee Brewers to win the World Series after they’d won the first two games of the series. “I’ll believe it when I see it” is the attitude people take when it comes to things like this, and I don’t blame them exactly.

Are pollsters herding? And if so, toward what?

On Still Counting, we discussed a Marist poll that came out this week and had some very weird results in Maine. This now feels like slightly old news. But the poll showed Troy Jackson ahead by 9 points among registered voters and the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Hannah Pingree, up by 11 among RVs. Among likely voters, however, Marist showed Jackson at a mere +2 — and Pingree tied against Republican Bobby Charles.

I’m not one to critique individual polls. Since we’re publishing a lot of newsletters, and since I tweet a lot, I think I’ve established some credibility on that front. But as I said on the show, I don’t think the Marist poll is defensible.

It’s not that Jackson +2 is infeasible. Indeed, it’s very close to FLIPR’s forecast in ME-SEN! What I don’t buy, though, is that Jackson would win by 9 points if every registered voter turns out, but is only slightly ahead given the actual likely-voter Maine electorate.

But ignore the Senate race for now, as important as it is. Marist’s gubernatorial poll in Maine makes absolutely zero sense.

For one thing, no other poll shows anything remotely in the vicinity of a tie in the governor’s race. Pingree leads by roughly 10 points in our polling average, which includes the Marist poll — but no other poll this cycle shows Pingree anything less than 8 points ahead:

The whole question in Maine is whether Collins has retained her supernatural powers to outperform polls and partisan baselines in a blue state in what looks like a very blue environment. I actually might take the under on FLIPR’s roughly 70/30 odds for Jackson.

There shouldn’t be much question, though, about Pingree being a heavy favorite in a fairly typical gubernatorial race. True, governor’s races are less correlated with the overall partisan environment than races for Congress, but Charles is a fairly obscure opponent whereas Pingree comes from a locally popular mini-dynasty.

The topline in Marist’s RV numbers was:

  • Pingree, 51 percent

  • Charles, 40 percent

  • Independent Rick Bennett, 7 percent

  • And 2 percent undecided.

Maine, unlike (say) South Carolina, is typically a high-turnout state, with somewhere in the neighborhood of 70 percent turnout among registered voters in recent midterms. But suppose that 70 percent of Charles RVs turn out, along with only 60 percent of Bennett’s supporters and undecided voters. This sort of spread is highly implausible, especially given that early voting looks decent-to-good for Democrats in Maine.

But humor me for a bit. Even with that correction applied, the topline would shift to Pingree 48, Charles 44. She’d still win.

I don’t see any way on earth that you have an 11-point shift from RV to LV in this relatively straightforward gubernatorial race, especially in what Marist itself sees as a D +8 national environment. On top of that, Marist has the undecided vote share in ME-GOV growing from 2 percent among registered voters to 6 percent among LVs. This makes even less sense. If you’re still undecided a week before the election, there’s a good chance that you won’t turn out at all. I’ve never seen a poll where the undecided ratio increased 3x when you filter for likely voters.

My leading hypothesis is that Marist, which does tend to publish relatively rosy numbers for Democrats, is terrified of its own shadow and/or terrified of being the next Ann Selzer, who was sued by President Trump. (The case was eventually dismissed.) The Senate race in Maine has a high profile; the gubernatorial race doesn’t. So it saw the Jackson +9 and it didn’t believe it, and then reverse-engineered its likely-voter model to produce a result that was more aligned with the consensus in Maine. And then its gubernatorial result was collateral damage.

My secondary hypothesis is that Marist’s spreadsheet or algorithm is broken and they ought to pay for some smart graduate students (or enough Claude or ChatGPT tokens) to fix it.

But if you’re issuing a survey that shows Pingree +11 and a tie in the same race in the same poll, you shouldn’t have published it.

Noah Wyhof-Rudnick has a great analysis of what pollsters are assuming about turnout shifts versus 2024. On average, the polls show a slightly more D-leaning turnout profile than two years ago, but only slightly.

You could argue that this is a conservative assumption given early voting data and other signs of Democratic enthusiasm. There’s also the potential issue, as Wyhof-Rudnick points out, of Trump voters mis-recalling or misstating their vote given how unpopular he has become, as some other pollsters have found. To simplify a bit, that could lead to these polls overestimating Republican turnout.

But, as Wyhof-Rudnick found, pollsters seem to be giving themselves varying degrees of permission to let their assumptions about turnout “float” relative to 2024, based on their priors about each race. They seem to be especially reluctant to underestimate Collins in Maine, given what happened in 2020.

This backs up my hypothesis, which is embedded into FLIPR, that pollsters are acutely aware of past polling errors and trying to correct for them — at the risk of either under-correcting or overcorrecting — and therefore the direction of polling error is hard to predict. Empirically, polling errors aren’t that correlated from cycle to cycle, but that might partly reflect how polling has become more of an art than a science. Human judgment plays a major role; as the Selzer Iowa poll in 2024 unfortunately showed, just “trusting your data” is no longer necessarily a reliable method.

Marist deserves credit for publishing both its RV and LV estimates, which most pollsters do not do. More often than not, the assumptions that pollsters make aren’t so transparent.

Still, I consider the Marist poll of Maine to be the “poll of the year.” Like Time Magazine's Person of the Year, this is sometimes an indicator of infamy, though. Pollsters seem to be undergoing a crisis of confidence and have a lot on the line (as do models like FLIPR). Polls are becoming something more like forecasts or models, rather than “pure” measures of public opinion. And models like FLIPR are becoming almost like prediction markets in basically taking a weighted average of those opinions. The Maine Senate race is a hard race to forecast. But I’m going to admit I’ll find it hilarious if Pingree wins by 10 points and Marist weighted its way out of what would otherwise have been an accurate result.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • We’ve patched FLIPR’s assumptions in the Montana Senate race, which is a weird one because there’s both an actual Democrat (Alani Bankhead) and a de facto Democrat (independent Seth Bodnar) on the ballot.

  • I’ve been doing lots of media, including being interviewed by Ezra Klein this week.

  • And please join us on Election Night!

Subscribe now

1

If you’re a pollster who happens to be reading this, please publish your surveys before 11:59 p.m. on Monday.

2

Subscribers to any of the four publications will have access to the liveblog.

3

Along with polls that aren’t officially Republican but usually lean that way.

4

Typically about 3-4 points of vote margin.

5

This actually featured the largest polling error of the Trump election triad.

6

Although not in FLIPR Classic and FLIPR Deluxe, which blend the polls with fundamentals and expert ratings, respectively.
